item.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the field of battle. The armies are drawn up and the moment of choice is heavy. He tells Arjuna that it is better to walk the path that is his own, even if it is flawed and uncertain, than to take up another's duty and perform it perfectly. The work that comes from your own nature, he says, carries its own rightness. It asks you to offer what you are, with all its limits, as the work itself.
item.for_you: You are trying to perform a role that was not yours to carry. The work of your own life is here, in the middle of your days. You are building your own thing, raising your children, and caring for your parents. That is your path.

item.for_you: The mind that replays your choice is your own mind, turning against itself. It is not an enemy outside of you. It is the part of you that is trying to understand, but is only finding the same old loop. You are not broken. You are a mind in a loop, and it is tired.

The body and its losses are temporary. This does not mean we should stop caring for those who are sick. It means the core of who you are remains, even when everything around you changes.
item.for_you: Your mother’s body went through a surgery, and that pain was real. But the part of you that loves her and the part of her that is not just a body are not defined by that moment. You can let the verdict against yourself loosen its grip.

item.line: Turn to doing good after a wrong, and you come out like the moon from behind a cloud.

item.for_you: You are doing the work you have. You are raising your children and building your life. That is your honest work. Let that be enough, and let it be the good you are doing now.

item.for_you: You are not defeated, only stretched. You have not settled for little. You are carrying a great deal. Set your mind on the good you are doing right now, and let that quiet the voice that says you did not do enough.

item.meaning: Krishna is showing Arjuna how to sit with his mind. He tells him that the mind will wander. When it does, Arjuna should gently guide it back. This is not a one-time fix. It is a practice of moderation and gentle return, again and again. The mind is like a lamp that needs steadying, and the work is simply to bring it home.
item.for_you: When you lie in bed and your mind is drafting tomorrow's emails, you do not need to fight it. You only need to notice where it has gone, and gently bring it back. This is your part. Do it again, and again, without force.

item.line: The mind runs here and there for nothing, wandering far like a stray village dog.

item.meaning: Nidagha is sitting with his teacher Ribhu. He is frustrated. He tells Ribhu that his mind runs here and there for no reason. It wanders far away, like a stray dog in a village. Ribhu listens. He knows that naming this restlessness is the first step toward understanding it. The wandering is not a failure. It is simply what the mind does.
item.for_you: You see the pattern now. Your mind runs here and there, chasing tomorrow, not because you are failing, but because it is its nature. Naming this is the beginning. It is not a verdict on you. It is simply the truth of what is happening.

item.line: Without understanding, the senses bolt like wild horses; with a steady mind, they run like trained ones.
item.translation: For one who lacks understanding, whose mind is never held steady, the senses run out of control like a driver's wild horses. For one who has understanding, whose mind is always steady, the senses obey like good horses.
item.why: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.
item.meaning: Yama is still speaking to Nachiketa, using the chariot to show what happens when a person is not awake inside themselves. The self is the rider. The body is the chariot. The intellect is the driver. The mind is the reins. The senses are the horses. If the mind is unsteady, the reins drop and the horses bolt. If the mind is steady, the horses obey and go where they are meant to go. The choice is always yours to hold the reins.
item.for_you: At night, your mind is the driver without reins. The phone is the horse running wild. Before you sleep, put the phone out of reach and sit still. Let your mind know it is safe to stop. Let it see the night is not a task to finish.

item.line: Why wander, mind? Rest. Not replaying the past, not scripting the future, I take what comes.
item.translation: Why do you wander about in vain, mind? Rest somewhere. Whatever is to happen happens just as it will, and not otherwise. Not recalling the past, not planning the future, I enjoy the pleasures that come to me unlooked-for.
item.why: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.
item.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own mind from a place of deep fatigue. He asks why it wanders in vain, replaying what is gone and scripting what is not yet here. He tells it to rest right where it is. He says whatever is to happen will happen, and he will take what comes without looking for it. The calm he wants is not somewhere else. It is here, in this moment, without the noise.
item.for_you: Tonight, when you feel the urge to draft tomorrow's emails, tell your mind what Bhartrihari told his: rest. What is to happen will happen. You have done your part for the day. Let the phone stay dark and let your mind simply be.

item.line: Let the monkey jump as much as he can; you simply wait and watch.
item.translation: The first lesson, then, is to sit for some time and let the mind run on. The mind is bubbling up all the time. It is like that monkey jumping about. Let the monkey jump as much as he can; you simply wait and watch. … But you will find that each day the mind's vagaries are becoming less and less violent, that each day it is becoming calmer.
item.why: Watch the mind before trying to control it; calm comes with daily practice.
item.meaning: Swami Vivekananda is teaching his students in New York about the first step with a racing mind. He says the mind is like a monkey, jumping and restless, full of thoughts and desires. You do not fight it. You simply sit and let it jump. You wait and watch. Each day you do this, the monkey jumps less. The mind grows calmer on its own, without force.
item.for_you: Tomorrow morning, sit for five minutes before you look at your phone. Let the monkey jump. Do not try to stop the thoughts. Just watch them. See what happens when you do not grab the reins but simply wait and watch.

item.meaning: Rama is speaking to the sages. He tells them that his mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and then a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming honestly what feels empty. The verse shows that naming what feels empty is the first step, and Rama's words are a question, not the answer. It turns gently toward your night, where the mind pounces on a fight and then drops it, leaving you restless.
item.for_you: Your mind is pouncing on the fight. See it for what it is: a restless mind looking for something to hold. You do not have to follow it into the dark.

item.line: Without understanding, the senses bolt like wild horses; with a steady mind, they run like trained ones.
item.translation: For one who lacks understanding, whose mind is never held steady, the senses run out of control like a driver's wild horses. For one who has understanding, whose mind is always steady, the senses obey like good horses.
item.why: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.
item.for_you: Your mind is running wild. You can hold the reins. Let your body rest now, and let the mind follow.

item.line: Like a tortoise pulling in its limbs, draw your senses back from what pulls at them.
item.translation: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side, a person withdraws the senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly set.
item.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.
item.meaning: Arjuna is asking what a steady person looks like, and Krishna answers. He says it is like a tortoise pulling its limbs in. A person takes their senses away from the things that pull at them. When they do this, their wisdom becomes steady. The mind is restless because it dwells on things. The next time you find yourself replaying the fight, you can see that the trouble is in what you are dwelling on. The verse suggests gently pulling your attention back, just as the tortoise does.
item.for_you: When the fight replays after lights out, see it as your senses wandering toward the words. You can pull your attention back to the feeling of the bed beneath you. Let your limbs rest. Let your mind settle into the room, not the argument.

item.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
item.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.
item.why: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.
item.meaning: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to settle the mind. He says the restless mind wanders, and wherever it goes, you bring it back. You do this again and again. The mind is not your enemy. It simply wanders. The practice is to gently guide it back to where you want it to be. It is a matter of returning, not of forcing it to stay.
item.for_you: When your mind wanders back to the fight, gently bring it back to the room. You do not need to fight the thought. You simply notice it and return to the quiet. Do this again and again.

item.line: Sit somewhere quiet, let the senses rest, and give your full attention to one thing.
item.translation: Sitting in a quiet place, senses at rest, self-mastered, pure within, one should contemplate the One with undivided attention, resting in the Self.
item.why: Quiet sitting and steady faith carry you until understanding becomes natural.
item.meaning: Lakshmana asks Rama how to cross the sea of confusion. Rama tells him to sit in a quiet place, let the senses rest, and give full attention to one thing. The mind becomes still like a calm ocean. Until understanding comes naturally, you rest in the Self. It is a practice of quiet sitting and steady faith.
item.for_you: Find a quiet place, even if it is just the bathroom after everyone sleeps. Let your senses rest. Give your full attention to one thing, like the sound of the fan. Let your mind rest there until it settles.

item.for_you: Notice the heaviness in your chest when you reach for the phone. That is the mood Krishna names. You do not have to fight it. Just name it as the heaviness it is, and let that be enough for tonight.

item.translation: The mind never really gets anything anywhere; even when great riches come, it never fills up inside, like a wicker basket dipped in water.

item.meaning: Rama sits with the sages and speaks of his own restless mind. He tells them the mind is like a wicker basket in water. You can pour in all the riches in the world, and the basket still never fills. It simply takes what is given and lets it wash through. He is naming the emptiness he feels, and he does not yet know how to fill it.
item.for_you: You open your phone for one minute and the night slips away. The wanting moves from one post to the next, never settling. This verse names that emptiness. See the basket for what it is, and do not blame the water for passing through.

item.line: When you stop chasing every desire and find contentment within yourself, your wisdom becomes steady.
item.translation: The Blessed Lord said: When a person gives up all the desires of the mind and is content in the self by the self, then he is called one of steady wisdom.
item.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.
item.meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna's question about the steady person. He describes someone who gives up chasing every desire. When a person finds contentment within, by the self alone, their wisdom becomes steady. Krishna is tracing how attention leads to anger and ruin, and how guarding it builds steadiness.
item.for_you: Your attention is the gate. When you guard it and do not chase every new thing, you build steadiness. This means choosing one thing to focus on, even for a short while, and letting the rest pass by.

item.line: No elixir and no fortune brings the happiness that inner calm brings.
item.translation: Not by drinking elixirs, not by the embrace of Lakshmi, does a person find such happiness as by calm within.
item.why: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.
item.meaning: Ribhu is speaking to Nidagha, who is looking for freedom. Ribhu tells him that no drink or wealth can match the calm inside. He says that sorrow and worry only leave when the mind is still. Restlessness is just the mind's habit, and only your own mind can quiet it. The quiet you find inside is the real treasure.
item.for_you: Your phone is not the enemy. The restless wanting is. When you close the app, you are not fighting a device. You are choosing to let your mind settle, just for one minute, and see what happens next.

item.meaning: Arjuna stands in his chariot and sees his own family lined up against him. He is about to fight a war he cannot bear to fight. His body gives way, his mouth goes dry, his limbs shake, and his hair stands on end. The text shows us a man frozen by grief and fear, not a hero stepping forward. It says that even the strongest among us can simply stop when the cost is too high.
item.for_you: You feel this in your body when the shouting starts and the door closes. Let the shaking be there. It is not a sign of weakness. It is your body telling you the cost is too high.

It is either something unwanted that happened, or a confused, wandering mind. There is no third source. He is saying that your pain is real. It comes from the violence you did not want, and from a mind that is spinning with fear. The days that have passed will not return. Grieve what you have lost. Then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

item.meaning: Tulsidas is frightened by the cruelty of the times. He tells Ram that he trusts and loves him, yet he is afraid. He asks Ram to speak the words he needs to hear. Ram tells him he is his. He says do not lose heart, do not tremble.

  title: Sita chooses to go
  characters: Sita, Ram
  opening: He came to tell her he was leaving for fourteen years; she told him she was coming.

  summary: Princess Savitri marries Satyavan knowing he will die within a year. On the fated day she follows Yama, the lord of death, speaking such wisdom about goodness and friendship that he grants boon after boon, until she wins back her husband's life.
  lesson: Steady love and clear speech can face even death. Determination carries what fear would drop.
